summary: Defines pre-shared key cipher suites for TLS that use stronger hashes (SHA-256 or SHA-384) and AES in Galois Counter Mode. Earlier PSK suites in RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 relied on SHA-1 in their message authentication code, so this gives newer options.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC adds TLS cipher suites for endpoints that already share a secret. Some use AES-GCM, and others replace SHA-1 with SHA-256 or SHA-384.

subtitle: New TLS pre-shared-key suites use AES-GCM or replace SHA-1 with SHA-256 or SHA-384.

tldr.problem: The earlier TLS pre-shared-key cipher suites used HMAC-SHA1, while the IETF was moving toward stronger hash algorithms.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines six AES-GCM suites for TLS 1.2 or later and twelve suites that use SHA-256 or SHA-384 with existing PSK key exchanges.
tldr.outcome: TLS can negotiate pre-shared-key suites using these updated algorithms. RFC 5487 is updated by RFC 10015.

today: RFC 5487 is a Proposed Standard, published in March 2009, and is updated by RFC 10015. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Why Add Pre-Shared-Key Suites
sections.content:
A pre-shared-key (PSK) cipher suite lets TLS endpoints authenticate with a symmetric secret they already share. RFC 4279 and RFC 4785 defined earlier PSK suites, but all of those suites used HMAC-SHA1 as their message authentication code.

TLS 1.2 added authenticated-encryption modes, including AES-GCM. RFC 5487 defines PSK suites using AES-GCM and suites that use SHA-256 or SHA-384 in place of SHA-1.
sections.plainLanguage: These suites let two TLS endpoints use a shared secret instead of public and private key pairs. They add newer encryption and hash choices to the existing PSK methods.

sections.title: TLS Versions for the Suites
sections.content:
The RFC defines two groups of suites with different version rules. The AES-GCM suites in Section 2 can be negotiated only with TLS 1.2 or higher. The SHA-256 and SHA-384 suites in Section 3 can be negotiated regardless of the negotiated TLS version.

The applicability statement in RFC 4279 also applies to these suites. The key exchanges themselves continue to follow the procedures defined for PSK, DHE_PSK, and RSA_PSK.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-GCM suites require TLS 1.2 or later. The other suites use the version rules of the earlier PSK specifications.

sections.title: AES-GCM Cipher Suites
sections.content:
Six cipher suites combine PSK, DHE_PSK, or RSA_PSK key exchange with AES-128-GCM or AES-256-GCM. They use the AEAD algorithms named in RFC 5116 and apply GCM as described in RFC 5288. The DHE_PSK suites provide Perfect Forward Secrecy.

Suites ending in _SHA256 use the TLS PRF with SHA-256, while those ending in _SHA384 use SHA-384. Implementations MUST send the TLS alert bad_record_mac for any failure while processing AES-GCM.
sections.plainLanguage: AES-GCM combines encryption and authentication for a record. The cipher-suite name also identifies the hash used by the TLS key-derivation function.

sections.title: SHA-256 and SHA-384 Suites
sections.content:
Twelve additional suites keep the PSK, DHE_PSK, and RSA_PSK key exchanges while changing the hash and PRF. Some use AES in CBC mode for confidentiality; others use NULL encryption and therefore provide integrity and authentication without confidentiality.

For a suite ending in _SHA256, HMAC uses SHA-256. For a suite ending in _SHA384, HMAC uses SHA-384. In TLS versions before 1.2, the PRF from that TLS version is used; otherwise the matching SHA-256 or SHA-384 TLS PRF applies.
sections.plainLanguage: These suites retain earlier key exchanges but use a different hash. The NULL-encryption options authenticate data without hiding it.

sections.title: Cipher-Suite Identifiers
sections.content:
IANA assigned two-byte identifiers to all eighteen suites. The six AES-GCM suites use values from 0x00,0xA8 through 0x00,0xAD. The twelve SHA-256 and SHA-384 suites use values from 0x00,0xAE through 0x00,0xB9.

Each endpoint uses these identifiers to select the same cipher suite during TLS negotiation. The RFC lists the mapping between each identifier and its suite name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each suite has an identifier that the endpoints can use to select matching TLS settings. The assigned values cover all eighteen suites.

sections.title: Confidentiality and Security
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4279, RFC 4785, and RFC 5288 apply. In particular, the suites with NULL encryption do not provide confidentiality, even though they provide integrity and authentication.

The RFC warns against sending sensitive information, such as passwords, over a connection using one of those NULL-encryption suites.
sections.plainLanguage: Some suites verify data without hiding it. Do not send passwords or other sensitive information over a connection that uses NULL encryption.
